source: Emery & Clayton (2004) The mentality of crows: convergent evolution of intelligence in corvids and apes. Science 306
finding: Review of corvid tool manufacture, mental time travel and social cognition. Proposes a cognitive tool kit of causal reasoning, flexibility, imagination and prospection shared by corvids and apes, evolved separately.
numbers: No new data. Abstract only.
limits: A review, not a test. Later work (b09, b10, b11) shows many causal-reasoning results can be explained by trial-and-error learning and feedback.
agent_relevance: Tool skill is a bundle of abilities. Our agent needs flexibility and foresight together with a tool library.

source: Weir, Chappell & Kacelnik (2002) Shaping of hooks in New Caledonian crows. Science 297
finding: Captive female crow Betty bent straight wire into a hook to lift a food bucket from a tube, after the only hooked wire was taken by her partner. First report of novel manufacture of a needed shape.
numbers: N=1 bird in the key manufacture trials. Exact trial counts not read this session.
limits: Single subject. Cannot separate insight from prior manipulation of the material. Abstract not available in the index; numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: A striking single case. Do not build agent design on one success; ask for repeated, controlled invention.

source: Kenward, Weir, Rutz & Kacelnik (2005) Behavioural ecology: tool manufacture by naive juvenile crows. Nature 433
finding: Hand-raised juvenile New Caledonian crows made and used tools with no adult contact and no human demonstration.
numbers: Abstract only. Sample size not read.
limits: Shows a strong inherited or self-taught part, not that tool shape is learned. Does not show regional standard shapes arise without social input.
agent_relevance: Some tool-making skill can arise from a strong prior plus play, not copying. Our agent may need a good starting library plus free exploration.

source: Hunt & Gray (2003) Diversification and cumulative evolution in New Caledonian crow tool manufacture. Proc R Soc B 270
finding: Survey found three standard pandanus tool designs (wide, narrow, stepped) with overlapping ranges and a shared manufacture method. Authors infer cumulative change from a common origin.
numbers: 5550 tools, 21 sites, 3 designs (abstract).
limits: Observational. Cultural transmission inferred, not shown. Later work (b12, b14) argues for individual learning plus a predisposition.
agent_relevance: Standardised designs spread as a few reusable templates. Matches a library of vetted helper tools instead of ad hoc tools each time.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Holzhaider & Gray (2007) Spontaneous metatool use by New Caledonian crows. Curr Biol 17
finding: Crows used a short tool to extract a longer tool that then got meat. Trial-and-error during the task and a previously learned rule were ruled out.
numbers: 7 crows; 6 of 7 first tried the short tool on the long tool; 4 got meat on trial 1 (abstract).
limits: Small sample. Authors favoured analogical reasoning. Later work (b08) asks whether it is planning or step-by-step feedback.
agent_relevance: Tools that fetch other tools are possible with few trials. Supports a two-level library: tools for getting tools.

source: Taylor, Hunt, Medina & Gray (2009) Do New Caledonian crows solve physical problems through causal reasoning? Proc R Soc B 276
finding: Three of six crows solved a two-trap trap-tube task. They avoided the trap when arbitrary cues were removed, but not when a hole and a functional trap were both present. They then solved a visually different trap-table task.
numbers: 3 of 6 crows solved the initial task; those 3 passed 4 transfers (abstract).
limits: Half the crows never solved it. The hole-plus-trap failure shows limits of the causal account.
agent_relevance: Transfer to a new look of the same problem is the real test. Test agent tools on re-skinned tasks, not the training ones.

source: von Bayern, Danel, Auersperg, Mioduszewska & Kacelnik (2018) Compound tool construction by New Caledonian crows. Sci Rep 8
finding: Naive crows were given short elements that could be joined into a long pole. Half made compound tools with no training. One made 3 and 4 piece tools. They chose compounds more often when food was far.
numbers: 8 crows tested; 4 of 8 succeeded in construction test 1 within about 4 to 6 min of interaction; unrewarded attempts before success: 0, 3, 7, 10. Need test: uncombined tool tried first on 70.8% of close trials vs 20.8% of distant trials. Fisher p = 0.037, 0.001, 0.100, 0.193 for the four birds. Rater agreement r = 0.993.
quote: Our results are not accountable by direct reinforcement learning
limits: Only 4 birds reached the need test, so no group statistics. The other 4 birds hardly ever tried to combine. Mechanism called opaque by authors.
agent_relevance: Tool making is rare even in a tool-using species: 50% made tools. Run many attempts and keep the winners. Building only when need is real is the gate our agent should have.

source: Gruber et al. (2019) New Caledonian crows use mental representations to solve metatool problems. Curr Biol 29
finding: Crows solved metatool problems where each stage was out of sight of the others, and ignored distractor apparatus. Authors call it the first conclusive evidence that birds plan several tool steps ahead.
numbers: 2017 criterion: 18 of 24 correct in two consecutive blocks. Stick condition after excluding trials with inspection while holding the tool: Aretha 12/14 correct (p=0.013), Freddie 14/18 (p=0.031). 2018 crows: Saturn 20/20, Triton 16/20. Two of the 2017 crows stayed significant under the strict test.
limits: Very small N. Birds were trained to criterion first, so it is trained planning. Only short chains tested.
agent_relevance: Foresight in tool chains is real but narrow. Plan sub-goals before calling a tool and check distractor tools, but keep chains short.

source: Jelbert, Taylor & Gray (2015) Investigating animal cognition with the Aesop's Fable paradigm. Commun Integr Biol 8
finding: Corvids pass many water-displacement tasks (water vs sand, heavy vs light, solid vs hollow) but fail counter-intuitive ones (U-tube). Two rivals are not ruled out: perceptual-motor feedback and object bias.
numbers: 6 NC crows with no stone experience: none spontaneously dropped stones. Rooks (with prior stone-dropping practice) did, some on trial 1. NC crows failed equal-level narrow vs wide tube with 12 objects; most passed with 4. Children pass the tasks at 5 to 7 years, the U-tube at 7 or over.
limits: Review of small-N studies. Success needed pre-training with stones.
agent_relevance: A result that vanishes when feedback or cues change is not understanding. Test agent tool use with cues removed and with distractor options.

source: Hennefield, Hwang, Weston & Povinelli (2018) Meta-analytic techniques reveal that corvid causal reasoning in the Aesop's Fable paradigm is driven by trial-and-error learning. Anim Cogn 21
finding: Pooled five articles. Birds learned from successful actions but not from unsuccessful ones, and did not transfer learning across tasks. Higher-order reasoning about mass, volume or displacement is unlikely.
numbers: 5 articles, over 32 experiments (abstract). Builds on Ghirlanda & Lind 2017, who reached a similar view from trial-level data.
limits: Abstract only read. Meta-analysis of small studies from a few groups. Does not cover manufacture such as hooks or compounds.
agent_relevance: Main failed-replication style warning. Learning from rewarded actions can look like reasoning. Log which agent tool successes were trial and error.

source: Azure-winged magpies in the Aesop's fable paradigm (2021) Sci Rep 11
finding: Magpies chose water over sand, heavy over light, solid over hollow, but failed on tube diameter, water level and the counter-intuitive U-tube. Choices were above chance only in the last trials, not the first.
numbers: Functional choices significant in the last 3 and 5 trials, not in the first 3 and 5 (Wilcoxon); preference emerged by about trial 20.
limits: Small group, one species. Authors say object bias had little effect.
agent_relevance: A rise across trials, not at trial 1, signals learning from feedback. Measure first-trial performance of a new tool skill to separate transfer from learning.

source: Exploring the role of individual learning in animal tool-use (2020) PeerJ
finding: Review of spontaneous acquisition of tool behaviours by naive animals. Argues the field over-weights social learning and under-reports individual learning.
numbers: Literature review across many species; counts not recorded here.
limits: Review of reports, with possible reporting bias. Social learning still sets frequencies.
agent_relevance: Agent tool skill may come from private trial and error with a good start. Sharing then spreads the winners (a shared library).

source: Acquisition of animal tool behaviour: baseline and social-learning conditions (2020) Phil Trans R Soc B
finding: Opinion piece. Proposes staged baseline and social-learning conditions to separate genetic bias, individual learning and copying in tool making.
numbers: No data. Proposes a method.
limits: Method only. Most field claims of culture lack such baseline conditions.
agent_relevance: Mirror this in our ablations: no library (baseline), own library, and library shared by others.

source: Auersperg et al. (2026) The flexible, the stereotyped and the in-between: combinatory tool use. Biol Rev 101
finding: Argues flexible vs stereotyped tool use is a spectrum. Inherited specialists can be flexible, and innovators can be limited. An intrinsic urge to combine objects underlies the onset of tool use.
numbers: Review; no new numbers read. Notes hooked-stick tools seem limited to specific crow populations with high individual variation.
limits: Hypothesis paper built on small experiments and observation.
agent_relevance: Playful object combination may seed tool invention. An agent could have a cheap combine-and-try step before it settles on a tool.

source: Rutz et al. (2016) Discovery of species-wide tool use in the Hawaiian crow. Nature 537
finding: Alala, extinct in the wild, showed species-wide proficient tool use. Juveniles developed functional tool use without training or adult input.
numbers: Abstract only. Counts not read.
limits: Captive birds only. Supports convergent evolution on islands.
agent_relevance: A second species with a built-in tool habit shows a strong prior can be enough. Fixed-form helpers can be good enough.

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer: language models can teach themselves to use tools. arXiv 2302.04761
finding: A language model learns when to call a calculator, QA system, search, translator and calendar, using self-made training data.
numbers: The ability to use provided tools emerges only at around 775M parameters; smaller models get similar results with or without tools.
limits: Tools are fixed and supplied. The model does not invent or store new tools.
agent_relevance: Tool use needs a minimum model size. Use of tools is not the same as making tools.

source: Cai, Wang, Ma, Chen & Zhou (2024) Large language models as tool makers (LATM). ICLR; arXiv 2305.17126
finding: A strong model (GPT-4) writes a reusable Python tool once. A weaker model (GPT-3.5) uses it many times. A dispatcher decides to reuse or make a new tool.
numbers: GPT-3.5 accuracy, chain-of-thought to LATM: Logical Deduction 66.4 to 79.7, Tracking Objects 61.6 to 99.6, Dyck 20.4 to 92.2, Word Sorting 59.2 to 98.3, Chinese Remainder 0.0 to 100.0, Schedule Meeting 18.9 to 100.0. GPT-4 with CoT: 88.8, 100, 63.6, 90.9, 0.0, 55.6. Cost O(nc+C) vs O(nC).
limits: Six code-friendly tasks. GPT-4 with LATM was slightly lower on Logical Deduction (86.6 vs 88.8).
agent_relevance: Closest analogue to a helper-tool library. Make once, use many gives big gains on code-friendly tasks. Check tasks where the tool does not help.

source: Qian et al. (2023) CREATOR: tool creation for disentangling abstract and concrete reasoning of LLMs. arXiv 2305.14318
finding: Splits work into creation, decision, execution and rectification. ChatGPT makes its own tools and beats chain-of-thought, program-of-thought and tool-use baselines.
numbers: ChatGPT: MATH 59.7%, TabMWP 94.7%, Creation Challenge 75.5%. TabMWP: Standard w/ CoT 75.2, PoT with rectification w/ CoT 87.3, Tool Use w/ CoT 79.6, CREATOR-Entangled w/ CoT 93.5. Creation hints raised Creation Challenge up to 18.7 points.
limits: ChatGPT only. Entangled variant was close on TabMWP (93.5 vs 94.7), so the split matters most on harder tasks. Rectification adds to success.
agent_relevance: Separating design of the tool from the decision to use it helped slightly. Fits a schema with separate make and use steps.

source: Yuan, Chen, Wang, Fung, Peng & Ji (2024) CRAFT: customizing LLMs by creating and retrieving from specialized toolsets. ICLR; arXiv 2309.17428
finding: GPT-4 solves training examples; solutions are validated, abstracted into snippets and deduplicated. At test time the model retrieves snippets. No fine-tuning.
numbers: 43.16% average relative F1 gain over best baselines on vision-language tasks. Performance rises with number of tools and model capability. Ablations show each component helps.
limits: Needs training examples and a strong creator model. Retrieval can bring in wrong tools. Gains were largest on vision-language tasks.
agent_relevance: Validation, abstraction and deduplication of tools each matter. A recipe for a pruned helper-tool library.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied lifelong learning agent with LLMs. arXiv 2305.16291
finding: Minecraft agent stores verified code skills in a growing library and reuses them. Automatic curriculum plus self-verification.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x more than baselines. Tech tree: wooden tool 15.3x faster, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x; only agent to reach diamond (1 of 3 runs, 102 iterations). Iron: Voyager 21 (SD 7) vs AutoGPT 135 (SD 103). ReAct and Reflexion 0/3 at every level. Random curriculum cuts items 93%. No self-verification: -73%.
limits: Three runs per method. Without the skill library the agent still reached iron in 3/3 runs (29 iterations) but plateaued later and never reached diamond. Needs GPT-4 for code quality.
agent_relevance: Library value grows as skills compound. Verifying a skill before storing it was the most important part.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: are large language models creative problem solvers? NAACL; arXiv 2311.09682
finding: 1,600+ problems that need unconventional use of objects. LLMs attempt more problems but often propose physically impossible actions. Step-wise reflection and divergent-convergent prompts help.
numbers: Majority of humans correct 79.3% vs GPT-4 73.3% (human evaluation). GPT-4: efficient solution 18.9%, infeasible 37.5%. Errors: wrong tool usage 42.4%, goal not achieved 17.7%, unfaithful to constraints 16.9%, unavailable tools 9.5%. Self-reflect cut infeasible by 9.7 points; divergent-convergent raised efficient by 6.5 points.
limits: Problems auto-generated with GPT-4 and human-checked; text only. Self-reflect did not help Claude 2 or Llama 2.
agent_relevance: The LLM weakness is the physical affordance of an object, like the crow trap-tube limits. Add an affordance check before using a tool.

source: Synthesis: tests that separate reasoning from learning in tool tasks
finding: Strongest discriminating tests in crow work: first-trial success (b07, b05), re-skinned transfer (b06), removing the feedback (b09), and out-of-sight stages (b08). Passing only after trials points to learning (b10, b11).
numbers: Sample sizes: compound tools 4 of 8 birds (b07); metatool 4 of 7 on trial 1 (b05); trap-tube 3 of 6 (b06).
limits: Synthesis by this agent from the lines cited; not a single paper.
agent_relevance: Apply these four tests to the agent: first use, re-skin, feedback removal, hidden stages.

source: Synthesis: library value depends on task type (LATM vs Voyager)
finding: Reuse gains are large where a task has one repeatable procedure and smaller where it needs open exploration.
numbers: LATM: up to +100 points for GPT-3.5 on six tasks. Voyager: no skill library still gave iron in 3/3 runs but 0/3 diamond vs 1/3 with library.
limits: Cross-paper comparison by this agent; settings differ.
agent_relevance: Expect library value on repeated or deep tasks, not one-off ones. Measure on both.

source: Synthesis: null model for tool-use claims (Hennefield 2018 plus Ghirlanda & Lind 2017)
finding: Initial preference for functional objects, plus learning from successes, can account for key Aesop results. This is a null model that a tool-use claim must beat.
numbers: 32+ experiments pooled; see b10.
limits: Abstract only for Hennefield; Ghirlanda & Lind 2017 not opened.
agent_relevance: Build a dumb baseline (preference plus learning from success) and require our tool method to beat it.

source: Jelbert et al. 2015: feedback dependence in string pulling and cranks
finding: String pulling needs visible incremental reward movement in crows, and apes solve a crank only with visible reward movement. The same logic is proposed for water tubes.
numbers: 11 NC crows all failed horizontal coiled string pulling where pulling did not bring the reward closer.
limits: Cited studies not opened.
agent_relevance: Hide intermediate feedback in some tests. If tool skill drops, it relied on feedback, not on a model of the problem.

source: von Bayern et al. 2018: transfer tests
finding: Birds that could build the compound tool transferred to new materials (straw, ground) within 2 attempts or fewer. Two made the compound in their first trial in the ground test.
numbers: Transfer 1: all 4 succeeded with at most 2 combinatory attempts. Transfer 2: all 4 built compounds in under 5 minutes; 2 succeeded on trial 1; one compound disintegrated.
limits: N=4 selected successful birds of 8.
agent_relevance: A tool concept that transfers across materials is worth storing as an abstract helper. Test that transfer.

source: Gruber et al. 2019: training and criterion
finding: Crows trained to criterion blocks. In 2018 trials stopped if a bird inspected an apparatus while holding the tool, so planning had to happen before action.
numbers: Criteria: 16 of 20 correct (2018 blocks); 18 of 24 in two consecutive blocks (2017).
limits: Criterion training means birds that never reached criterion are not part of the claim.
agent_relevance: State the share of runs that never reach criterion when reporting tool methods.
